explanations.explanation: Suppress is the word. Paul, the apostle writing this letter to believers in Rome, says these are men "who suppress the truth by their wickedness." You know that move where you hold a beach ball underwater? It takes effort, and it keeps wanting to pop right back up. The truth is right there, and they're sitting on it.

Seek is a friendly word, and that's why it's tempting. But Paul says they "suppress the truth by their wickedness." Suppressing means pushing something down, which is about as far from going out looking for it as you can get. Easy one to slide past, friend.

Spreading is what my sprinkles do when somebody bumps the jar, and it sounds like a busy, active word. But Paul says they "suppress the truth by their wickedness." That's pressing it down, not sending it out. The truth isn't getting passed around in this verse.

True. Paul says, "For what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them." Notice who does the making plain. It isn't the people figuring it out on their own. God did it.

This one is true, and the text says it directly: "For what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them." Paul doesn't say it's hidden or hard to find. He says God made it plain. I know "plain" can sound too good to be true, but that's what the verse says.

Workmanship is right. Paul says God's invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, are "understood from His workmanship." God can't be seen, but what He made can. It's like how you can tell a lot about a cook from one look at the cookie tray.

Commandments is a good guess, since we think of God's character when we think of His rules. But here Paul points somewhere else. He says these qualities have been seen "since the creation of the world," and they're understood from His workmanship. That means what He made.

Messengers makes sense, since God does send people with words, and I've met an angel myself. But this verse doesn't mention any messengers. Paul says God's invisible qualities are "understood from His workmanship." The evidence is what He made.

Without excuse is exactly what Paul says. God's invisible qualities "have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse." Clearly seen leaves very little room for "I had no idea." It's like telling the boss the report was due Friday after it's been on your calendar in red.

Waiting for proof sounds fair at first. But Paul says God's qualities have been "clearly seen" since the creation of the world. The proof isn't missing. That's why he ends with people being "without excuse."

explanations.answer: They are unable to know Him
explanations.explanation: That's a sympathetic answer, but Paul says the opposite. "What may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them" (Romans 1:19). If it's plain, they aren't stuck in the dark. That's how Paul gets to "without excuse."

It's an easy thing to assume, but Paul says the opposite. He writes, "For although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him." They knew Him. The trouble came after that.
False, and good catch. Paul says, "although they knew God." So the problem wasn't that they never knew Him. They knew Him and still didn't glorify Him as God or give thanks.
That's it. Paul says "they became futile in their thinking and darkened in their foolish hearts." Futile means it goes nowhere. Think of a hamster wheel that's very busy and very sure of itself.

Fearful and troubled sounds like a natural result, but it isn't what the verse says. Paul says "they became futile in their thinking and darkened in their foolish hearts." Nothing in the verse says they felt afraid. Futile is thinking that goes nowhere, and darkened is the heart.

Divided and restless could sound right if you picture a mind pulled two ways. But Paul's words are "futile in their thinking and darkened in their foolish hearts." He doesn't say they were torn or restless. He says their thinking got futile and their hearts got dark.

explanations.answer: Images of mortal man and animals
explanations.explanation: Right. Paul says they "exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles." Look at the two sides of that trade. On one side is the immortal God, and on the other are images of things that die.

Gold and silver is a common thing to trade for, but it's not in this verse. Paul says they exchanged God's glory "for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles." It's a strange list, and that's the point.
I can see why that came to mind, since people chase praise all the time. But Paul doesn't mention kings or their praise here. The trade is "images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles."

That's what the text says: "Therefore God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity for the dishonoring of their bodies with one another." This is a heavy verse, and I think it's meant to be. Notice that it says God gave them over. He didn't send a disaster.

explanations.answer: Sends a flood to wipe them out
explanations.explanation: A flood did happen in the Bible, in Noah's day (Genesis 6:17). Noah, by the way, was the man God told to build an ark. But that's a different passage. Here the text says, "God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity."

explanations.answer: Sends a prophet to warn them
explanations.explanation: Sending a prophet sounds like a kind and reasonable next step. But this passage doesn't mention one. After the trade, the text says "Therefore God gave them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity."

Creature is the word. Paul says they "worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator." Same letters, one big difference. It's like swapping the person who baked your cookies for the cookie.

Law is a reasonable guess, since Paul writes a lot about it in this letter. But here he says they "worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator." The contrast is between what was made and the One who made it.

Covenant is a big Bible word, so it's a tempting pick. But it isn't in this verse. Paul says they "worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator." The choice is between what was made and the One who made it.
True. Paul says the Creator "is forever worthy of praise! Amen." Right in the middle of a heavy passage, he stops to say that. Some things get said out loud no matter what else is going on.

It's true, and you can see it right in the text. After he mentions the Creator, Paul writes that He "is forever worthy of praise! Amen." He doesn't wait until the end of the chapter. He says it right there.

Yes. Paul says, "since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, He gave them up to a depraved mind." It's a heavy phrase, and I think it's meant to land that way. The verse ties the giving up to their not acknowledging God.
A final warning is a pretty natural guess. It's what we'd expect from a patient father. But Paul says, "He gave them up to a depraved mind." There's no warning in this verse.

A time of testing sounds like a sensible next step, and the Bible does talk about testing in other places. But in this verse Paul says, "He gave them up to a depraved mind." Nothing in it says anything about a test.
True. Paul says God gave them up to a depraved mind, "to do what ought not to be done." The mind leads to the actions. It's like how a bad map leads to a bad drive.
This one is true. The verse says He gave them up to a depraved mind "to do what ought not to be done." So the mind and the doing go together in Paul's words.
It sounds like a believable claim, but Paul says the opposite. In his list he writes, "They invent new forms of evil." So they aren't just repeating the old stuff. They keep coming up with new ones.
False, and you caught it. In his list Paul writes, "They invent new forms of evil." So the text says they do invent new ones. That's quite a list to be on.

explanations.answer: Keep going and approve of others
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, "they not only continue to do these things, but also approve of those who practice them." Knowing the decree didn't stop them. They kept going and cheered others on, which is a hard thing to read.

explanations.answer: Stop and turn back to God
explanations.explanation: Turning back would be a hopeful ending, and I wish the verse said it. But Paul says, "they not only continue to do these things, but also approve of those who practice them." They knew the decree and kept going.

explanations.answer: Hide it from everyone around them
explanations.explanation: Hiding is the usual move when someone knows they're in the wrong. But Paul says something different here. They "continue to do these things, but also approve of those who practice them." Nothing in the verse says they hid it.
